claims.text: Differences in deformation and failure behavior among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its ternary and quaternary subsets are primarily governed by variations in local chemical short-range order and stacking-fault energy.
The investigated quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys have single-phase FCC microstructures after comparable thermomechanical processing.
Changing alloy composition changes the degree of local chemical ordering.
Local chemical short-range order modulates stacking-fault energy.
Increased short-range order lowers stacking-fault energy in some subsets.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes deformation twinning.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes complex dislocation interactions.
Twinning and complex dislocation interactions delay strain localization.
Delayed strain localization enhances strength and work hardening.
Less pronounced short-range order produces higher stacking-fault energy.
Higher stacking-fault energy favors easier conventional dislocation glide.
Easier dislocation glide results in lower strain hardening and lower strength.
Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, subsets with greater local ordering will have higher yield strength and work hardening.
Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, subsets with lower local ordering will have lower strength.
Subsets with lower local ordering may have greater ductility because dislocation glide is less hindered.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys subjected to similar thermomechanical histories.
The proposed mechanism may not govern multiphase alloys or alloys dominated by precipitation or grain-boundary engineering.
Magnetic interactions or residual stresses could confound attribution of mechanical behavior solely to short-range order.
